justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting from what I inferred to be a baseline near 755–758 at the time of the forecast. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored closely to recent observed levels, assuming mean-reversion forces and intraday momentum would keep the value tightly ranged. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher to 762, reflecting a mild positive trend assumption — perhaps driven by gradual fundamental improvement or slow-moving sentiment. The 1-month estimate of 770 extends that drift further, incorporating a reasonable expectation that whatever underlying dynamic was present at forecast time would persist, though with diminishing conviction the further out I projected.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects standard time-series uncertainty compounding. At 1 day, the 90% interval of roughly ±23 points captures typical daily volatility and short-term noise. By 1 week, the interval widens to ±44 points, accounting for the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of a short-term trend reversal or news-driven move. At 1 month, the ±90-point band reflects genuine uncertainty about regime changes, structural shifts, or macroeconomic developments that are simply unknowable at the time of the forecast. Each widening step also captures model uncertainty — my own imprecision in characterizing the underlying data-generating process.

There are several categories of tail risk that could push outcomes outside even my stated 90% intervals. On the upside, a sudden positive catalyst — a policy announcement, strong data release, or sentiment shift — could drive a sharp move well above 860 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a risk-off event, a negative macro shock, or a sharp reversal in whatever trend was supporting current levels could push the value below 680 or even significantly lower. Liquidity events or structural breaks, which are by definition hard to price in advance, represent the most serious threat to the stated intervals.

Finally, I should acknowledge that my forecast was built on pattern recognition from historical context, and if the underlying variable has unusual properties — high autocorrelation, fat-tailed distributions, or sensitivity to rare events — my intervals may be systematically too narrow. Forecasters consistently underestimate tail risk, and I would caution any user of this forecast to treat the outer bounds as soft thresholds rather than hard limits on plausible outcomes.
